Rank, Head-Channel Non-Identifiability, and Symmetry Breaking:
A Precise Analysis of Representational Collapse in Transformers

Giansalvo Cirrincione Email: exin@u-picardie.fr Address: Laboratoire LTI, Université de Picardie Jules Verne, Chemin du Thil, 80025 Amiens, France
Abstract

A widely cited result by Dong et al. (2021) showed that Transformer architectures built from self-attention alone, without skip connections or feed-forward layers, suffer from rapid rank collapse: all token representations converge to a single direction, destroying the model’s expressive capacity. The proposed remedy was the MLP sub-layer. It is shown in this paper that this picture, while correct in the specific regime studied by Dong, is incomplete in ways that matter for architectural understanding and design.

Three results are established. First, layer normalisation is precisely affine-rank-neutral: it preserves the affine rank of the token representation set exactly, and preserves matrix rank in the zero-bias case. It neither contributes to nor mitigates rank collapse. The widespread claim that layer normalisation “plays no role” is imprecise; the correct statement is sharper. Second, residual connections generically obstruct rank collapse in real Transformer architectures such as BertBase, without any contribution from the MLP. The MLP’s irreplaceable function is a different one: generating feature directions that lie outside the linear span of the original token embeddings, which no stack of attention layers can produce. Third, a phenomenon distinct from rank collapse is identified and characterised: head-channel non-identifiability. When multi-head attention aggregates the outputs of individual heads by summation through the output projection matrix, the per-head contributions become irrecoverable from the mixture. No downstream component, including the MLP, can undo this loss of identity, because the MLP receives only the already-mixed signal.

These three results lead to a design corollary: the standard choice of feed-forward width equal to four times the model dimension is an engineering heuristic whose justification is neither rank preservation nor expressiveness in general. The correct width depends on the non-linear complexity of the task and on the degree of head specialisation, which determines how much rank contraction the multi-head output undergoes before reaching the MLP.

A constructive partial remedy for head-channel non-identifiability is proposed in the form of a position-gated output projection, and a verifiable empirical prediction is stated. Finally, a unifying algebraic framework is presented: all four collapse phenomena identified in the recent literature — rank collapse in depth, rank collapse in width, head-channel non-identifiability, and entropy collapse — correspond to distinct symmetries of the Transformer’s forward pass that the standard architecture fails to break.

Keywords: 
attention mechanism , rank collapse , head-channel non-identifiability , layer normalisation , residual connections , MLP , Transformer

1 Introduction

In a landmark result, Dong et al. [4] showed that iterating the attention operation without any other mechanism causes the hidden states to collapse to a rank-1 matrix doubly exponentially in depth. The paper frames the role of the MLP as the antagonist in a “tug of war”: attention reduces rank, MLP restores it.

This picture captures something real. It also leaves three important questions unanswered, each with architectural consequences.

Three gaps

(i) What does layer normalisation actually do to rank? Dong says it “plays no role.” This is not quite right: LN is not passive, it is exactly neutral — it preserves rank precisely, neither helping nor hindering. The distinction matters when using rank to measure representational capacity across layers.

(ii) Does the MLP need to generically obstruct rank collapse in real Transformers, which have residual connections? The residual update X(l+1)=X(l)+Δ(l)X^{(l+1)}=X^{(l)}+\Delta^{(l)} can only increase rank in the generic case. Residual connections generically obstruct collapse. The MLP’s necessary function is therefore something else entirely: generating non-linear features that the bilinear attention mechanism cannot reach.

(iii) Is rank collapse the only threat to representational capacity? An identification is made a second, distinct phenomenon: head-channel non-identifiability. After multi-head attention computes HH specialised outputs and sums them through the output projection, their individual contributions can no longer be canonically attributed to a specific functional head. The MLP operates on this already-mixed representation and cannot recover the per-head decomposition. This is not a variant of rank collapse — it is a different problem, with a different cause and a different remedy.

Contributions

  1. (i)

    Rank-Neutrality Theorem (§4): arank⁡(LN⁡(X))=arank⁡(X)\operatorname{arank}(\operatorname{LN}(X))=\operatorname{arank}(X) under non-degeneracy hypotheses; matrix rank is preserved in the zero-bias case.

  2. (ii)

    Residual rank stability (§5): rank collapse does not occur in BERT-like architectures with residual connections; the MLP is sufficient but not necessary for this purpose.

  3. (iii)

    Head-Channel Non-Identifiability Theorem (§7): the per-head contributions to multi-head attention output are irrecoverable from their sum; the MLP does not remedy this.

  4. (iv)

    Design corollary (§6, A): dff=4​dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}=4d_{\mathrm{model}} is an engineering heuristic; the right quantity is the non-linear complexity of the task.

  5. (v)

    PG-OP (§8): a position-gated output projection that partially addresses head-channel non-identifiability at less than 1.6% of WOW_{O}’s parameter count, with a verifiable empirical prediction.

  6. (vi)

    Recovery Ambiguity Theorem (§7.3): the exact recovery ambiguity dimension of head-channel non-identifiability is n⁡(H−1)​dkn(H-1)d_{k} degrees of freedom per layer. For BertBase: 360,448360{,}448 per sequence (or 704704 per token) per layer.

  7. (vii)

    Rank Contraction Theorem (§6): head specialisation causes rank contraction in MHA⁡(X)\operatorname{MHA}(X); the MLP must expand exactly the directions the heads contracted. This gives the first principled lower bound on dffd_{\mathrm{ff}}.

  8. (viii)

    Symmetry-Breaking Framework (partially proved) (§9): all four collapse phenomena are orbits of the invariance group 𝒢\mathcal{G} of the Transformer. The design question “what components are needed?” reduces to “what symmetries must be broken?”

Relationship with Dong et al

The results do not contradict Dong. In the regime they study — pure attention, no residual, no MLP — rank collapse occurs as they prove. The study concerns the regime of actual deployed Transformers (BERT, GPT), where residual connections are present. The gap between the two regimes is the source of all three discrepancies above.

Dong’s setup

Dong et al. [4] study the map X↦A(1:L)XWV(1:L)WO(1:L)X\mapsto A^{(1:L)}XW_{V}^{(1:L)}W_{O}^{(1:L)} with A(l)A^{(l)} row-stochastic (uniform attention). No residual connections. No MLP. Under these conditions, the product of stochastic matrices converges to a rank-1 matrix doubly-exponentially in LL. With MLP and residual, the rank is maintained.

The three issues at a glance

The following scheme summarises the three corrections developed in this paper, ordered by the component they concern:

Component Dong (2021) This paper
Layer normalisation Plays no role Preserves affine rank exactly; matrix rank in zero-bias case
Residual connections One of two remedies Generically obstruct collapse
MLP Necessary (anti-collapse) Necessary only for non-linearity
Output projection WOW_{O} Not discussed Induces head-channel non-identifiability

Each row corresponds to one section of the paper: §4 addresses layer normalisation, §5 the residual connections and MLP, §7 the output projection.

3 Related Work

Rank collapse in depth (Dong et al., 2021)

Dong et al. [4] proved that pure self-attention without residual connections converges to rank 1 doubly-exponentially in depth. They note that skip connections mitigate collapse, but treat the effect as approximate. Theorem 5.3 (Residual Rank Obstruction) makes the generic obstruction statement precise.

Skip connections and large weights

A recent preprint [21] shows that only large weights (together with skip connections) can prevent the perils of rank collapse, providing conditions under which skip connections alone fail. This is consistent with our Proposition 5.1: rank increase under residual updates is generic but not unconditional — rank non-decrease holds generically (Proposition 5.1), which can fail if weights are near zero.

LayerNorm and rank collapse (Wu et al., NeurIPS 2024)

Wu et al. [16] provide the most precise treatment of LayerNorm prior to this work. They prove that for certain classes of value matrices, attention with LayerNorm still collapses exponentially. For masked and sparse attention, they show LayerNorm can slow collapse. Their conclusion is that LayerNorm has a complex, regime-dependent effect on rank. Our Rank-Neutrality Theorem (Theorem 4.2) gives the complementary result: with respect to rank specifically (not convergence rate), LayerNorm is exactly transparent under H1–H2 — it preserves rank precisely. These two results together give a complete picture: LN neither prevents collapse (our theorem) nor accelerates it; the collapse rate is controlled by other factors (Wu et al.).

LayerNorm in MLPs (Joudaki et al., NeurIPS 2023)

Joudaki et al. [17] show LN can generically obstruct rank collapse in MLP networks; this does not extend to self-attention due to softmax coupling. The Rank-Neutrality Theorem gives the exact self-attention result.

Rank collapse in width (Nait Saada et al., 2024)

Nait Saada et al. [18] identify a third type of rank collapse, distinct from depth collapse and from head-channel non-identifiability: rank collapse in width, occurring as context length nn increases within a single attention layer. Using random matrix theory, they show that a spectral gap between the two largest singular values of the attention matrix drives this phenomenon. This is orthogonal to all three contributions of the present paper: depth collapse is addressed by Theorem 5.3 (Residual Rank Obstruction), head-channel non-identifiability by Theorem 7.3, and neither concerns width collapse. We discuss the taxonomy of all four collapse types in §10 and §11.

MLP as key-value memory (Geva et al., 2021)

Geva et al. [6] show that MLP layers function as key-value memories storing factual associations. The analysis is orthogonal: we address the structural role of the MLP in rank maintenance and non-linear feature generation, not its functional role in storing factual knowledge.

Signal propagation and entropy collapse

Noci et al. [19] extend Dong’s analysis to the training dynamics, showing that rank collapse at initialisation causes vanishing gradients. Zhai et al. [20] identify entropy collapse (attention concentrating on too few tokens) as a distinct failure mode. Both are orthogonal to head-channel non-identifiability.

4 The Rank-Neutrality Theorem

Layer normalisation maps each row xix_{i} as:

LN⁡(xi)=xi−x¯iσi⊙γ+β,\operatorname{LN}(x_{i})=\frac{x_{i}-\bar{x}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}}\odot\gamma+\beta, (1)

where x¯i=1dmodel​∑jxi​j\bar{x}_{i}=\frac{1}{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\sum_{j}x_{ij}, σi2=1dmodel​∑j(xi​j−x¯i)2+ϵ\sigma_{i}^{2}=\frac{1}{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\sum_{j}(x_{ij}-\bar{x}_{i})^{2}+\epsilon, and γ,β∈ℝdmodel\gamma,\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}} are learned affine parameters.

Dong et al. [4] state that LN “plays no role” in preventing rank collapse. The following theorem gives the precise statement.

Definition 4.1 (Non-degeneracy).

Matrix X∈ℝn×dmodelX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} and learned scale parameters γ∈ℝdmodel\gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}} satisfy:

  • H1

    No row of XX is constant: σi>0\sigma_{i}>0 for all ii.

  • H2

    The all-ones vector is not in the row space of XX: 𝟏∉rowspace⁡(X)\mathbf{1}\notin\operatorname{rowspace}(X).

  • H3

    All scale parameters are non-zero: γj≠0\gamma_{j}\neq 0 for all j=1,…,dmodelj=1,\ldots,d_{\mathrm{model}}.

H3 holds at any reasonable initialisation of γ\gamma (e.g. γ=𝟏\gamma=\mathbf{1}) and is preserved by standard optimisers unless a component is explicitly driven to zero.

Theorem 4.2 (Rank-Neutrality Theorem).

Let arank⁡(S)\operatorname{arank}(S) denote the affine rank of a set of row vectors S={x1,…,xn}⊂ℝdS=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, defined as arank⁡(S)=rank⁡(X−x1​𝟏⊤)\operatorname{arank}(S)=\operatorname{rank}(X-x_{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}) where rows of XX are the elements of SS. Under H1, H2, H3, and H4 (σ∉colspace⁡(X~)\sigma\notin\mathrm{colspace}(\tilde{X}), where σi=σ⁡(xi)\sigma_{i}=\sigma(x_{i}) and X~=X​P\tilde{X}=XP):

arank⁡(LN⁡(X))=arank⁡(X).\operatorname{arank}(\operatorname{LN}(X))=\operatorname{arank}(X).

Moreover, if β=𝟎\beta=\mathbf{0} (standard initialisation), then also rank⁡(LN⁡(X))=rank⁡(X)\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{LN}(X))=\operatorname{rank}(X).

Remark 4.3 (On hypothesis H4).

Hypothesis H4 (σ∉colspace⁡(X~)\sigma\notin\mathrm{colspace}(\tilde{X}), where σi=σ⁡(xi)\sigma_{i}=\sigma(x_{i}) are the row-wise standard deviations and X~=X​P\tilde{X}=XP) excludes the exceptional case in which the vector of standard deviations is representable as a linear combination of the centred token coordinates. This is the unique situation in which row-wise radial rescaling can collapse an affine independence relation. The condition holds for all inputs satisfying n>dn>d (the common case, since sequences are longer than the embedding dimension), and generically for n≤dn\leq d. All four hypotheses H1–H4 are mild non-degeneracy conditions that hold at standard initialisation and are maintained during training under normal operating conditions.

Remark 4.4 (Matrix rank vs affine rank).

The distinction between matrix rank and affine rank matters here. The affine rank of the row set is the correct invariant: mean subtraction in Step 1 removes the constant component, so the natural rank to track is that of the centred matrix. The matrix rank rank⁡(LN⁡(X))\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{LN}(X)) can exceed rank⁡(X)\operatorname{rank}(X) by at most one (when β≠𝟎\beta\neq\mathbf{0} has a non-zero mean component), but the affine rank is exactly preserved. This is the statement that matters for representational capacity: the effective dimensionality of the token representation set is unchanged by layer normalisation.

Proof.

Let S={x1,…,xn}S=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\} be the row set of XX. The affine rank is arank⁡(S)=rank⁡(X−x1​𝟏⊤)\operatorname{arank}(S)=\operatorname{rank}(X-x_{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}), i.e. the dimension of the affine span of SS.

Step 1 (mean subtraction). LN first computes x~i=xi−x¯i​𝟏⊤\tilde{x}_{i}=x_{i}-\bar{x}_{i}\mathbf{1}^{\top}, i.e. X~=X​P\tilde{X}=XP where P=I−d−1​𝟏𝟏⊤P=I-d^{-1}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}. The affine span of {xi}\{x_{i}\} equals the linear span of {xi−x1}i≥2\{x_{i}-x_{1}\}_{i\geq 2}. Since x~i−x~1=(xi−x1)−(x¯i−x¯1)​𝟏⊤\tilde{x}_{i}-\tilde{x}_{1}=(x_{i}-x_{1})-(\bar{x}_{i}-\bar{x}_{1})\mathbf{1}^{\top}, the affine span of {x~i}\{\tilde{x}_{i}\} is a subset of 𝟏⟂\mathbf{1}^{\perp}. By H2, 𝟏∉rowspace⁡(X)\mathbf{1}\notin\operatorname{rowspace}(X), so rank⁡(X​P)=rank⁡(X)\operatorname{rank}(XP)=\operatorname{rank}(X) (the projection is injective on rowspace⁡(X)\operatorname{rowspace}(X)). Hence arank⁡(S~)=arank⁡(S)\operatorname{arank}(\tilde{S})=\operatorname{arank}(S).

Step 2 (row-wise rescaling by 1/σi1/\sigma_{i}). Let D=diag⁡(1/σ1,…,1/σn)D=\mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma_{1},\ldots,1/\sigma_{n}), σi>0\sigma_{i}>0 by H1. The affine rank decreases under DD if and only if σ=(σ1,…,σn)⊤∈colspace⁡(X~)\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n})^{\top}\in\mathrm{colspace}(\tilde{X}), i.e. there exists v≠0v\neq 0 with X~​v=c​σ\tilde{X}v=c\,\sigma for some c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}. (H4 holds generically when n>dn>d, since colspace⁡(X~)\mathrm{colspace}(\tilde{X}) has dimension at most d≪nd\ll n.)

(3a) Right-multiplication by diag⁡(γ)\mathrm{diag}(\gamma) is an invertible linear map (γj≠0\gamma_{j}\neq 0 by H3), hence preserves affine rank: arank⁡({yi−β})=arank⁡(S^)\operatorname{arank}(\{y_{i}-\beta\})=\operatorname{arank}(\hat{S}). For the matrix-rank statement: when β=𝟎\beta=\mathbf{0}, Step 3b is trivial and rank⁡(LN⁡(X))=rank⁡(X^​diag​(γ))=rank⁡(X)\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{LN}(X))=\operatorname{rank}(\hat{X}\,\mathrm{diag}(\gamma))=\operatorname{rank}(X) by Steps 1–2 and the invertibility of diag⁡(γ)\mathrm{diag}(\gamma). ∎

Remark 4.5 (Comparison with the literature and scope of H1–H3).

Three positions on LayerNorm and rank have appeared recently:

  • •

    Dong et al. [4]: LN “plays no role.” (Imprecise — it is rank-neutral, which is a stronger and more precise statement.)

  • •

    Wu et al. [16]: LN can slow collapse in certain regimes. (True for convergence rate; our result concerns rank preservation at each step.)

  • •

    Joudaki et al. [17]: LN prevents rank collapse in MLPs. (True there; here it is shown to be rank-neutral, neither helping nor hindering.)

The hypotheses H1–H4 are mild in practice. H1 (no constant row) fails only at degenerate initialisation. H2 (𝟏∉rowspace⁡(X)\mathbf{1}\notin\operatorname{rowspace}(X)) holds with probability one at random initialisation and is robustly maintained during training. H3 (γj≠0\gamma_{j}\neq 0) holds at the standard initialisation γ=𝟏\gamma=\mathbf{1} and is preserved unless training explicitly drives a scale to zero, which is penalised by weight decay. Under these conditions, LN is exactly rank-preserving: the tug of war between attention and MLP operates with LN as a transparent bystander.

5 Residual Connections and the MLP’s Actual Role

5.1 Rank under residual updates

Proposition 5.1 (Generic rank non-collapse under additive perturbation).

For any A,B∈ℝn×dmodelA,B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} the rank triangle inequality

|rank⁡(A)−rank⁡(B)|≤rank⁡(A+B)≤rank⁡(A)+rank⁡(B)|\operatorname{rank}(A)-\operatorname{rank}(B)|\;\leq\;\operatorname{rank}(A+B)\;\leq\;\operatorname{rank}(A)+\operatorname{rank}(B) (2)

holds, and no deterministic lower bound stronger than (2) exists: setting B=−AB=-A gives rank⁡(A+B)=0\operatorname{rank}(A+B)=0.

The following generic statement, however, holds. Fix A∈ℝn×dmodelA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} with rank⁡(A)=r<min⁡(n,dmodel)\operatorname{rank}(A)=r<\min(n,d_{\mathrm{model}}), and let μ\mu be any probability measure on ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} that is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Then

PrB∼μ[rank(A+B)>r]=1.\Pr_{B\sim\mu}\bigl[\operatorname{rank}(A+B)>r\bigr]=1. (3)
Proof.

The triangle inequality (2) is standard. For (3), the determinantal variety

𝒱r={M∈ℝn×dmodel:rank⁡(M)≤r}\mathcal{V}_{r}\;=\;\{M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}:\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq r\}

is the common zero set of the (r+1)×(r+1)(r{+}1)\times(r{+}1) minors of MM, hence a closed real-algebraic set. Since r<min⁡(n,dmodel)r<\min(n,d_{\mathrm{model}}), it has codimension (n−r)​(dmodel−r)≥1(n-r)(d_{\mathrm{model}}-r)\geq 1, and is therefore of Lebesgue measure zero in ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. The set {B:rank⁡(A+B)≤r}=𝒱r−A\{B:\operatorname{rank}(A+B)\leq r\}=\mathcal{V}_{r}-A is its translate, which has Lebesgue measure zero by translation invariance of Lebesgue measure. Any μ\mu absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue therefore assigns it zero mass. ∎

Remark 5.2.

Four points are worth noting. (i) The statement is asymmetric in AA and BB: AA is held fixed and BB is the absolutely continuous perturbation. This is precisely the regime relevant to residual updates, where A=X(l)A=X^{(l)} is the current state and B=Δ(l)B=\Delta^{(l)} is the update. (ii) If AA is already full-rank, r=min⁡(n,dmodel)r=\min(n,d_{\mathrm{model}}) and the proposition is vacuous: the rank cannot increase further. The proposition is non-trivial precisely in the rank-deficient regime, which is the regime of rank collapse. (iii) The condition rowspace⁡(Δ(l))⊈rowspace⁡(X(l))\operatorname{rowspace}(\Delta^{(l)})\not\subseteq\operatorname{rowspace}(X^{(l)}) is sufficient but not necessary for rank to strictly increase, and is itself generic: its negation defines an algebraic variety of Lebesgue measure zero, recovered as a special case of the argument above. (iv) The proposition assumes BB is absolutely continuous on ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. When BB is constrained to a lower-dimensional sub-manifold—as is the case for B=MHA⁡(X)B=\operatorname{MHA}(X), which depends analytically on XX and on the attention weights—the conclusion no longer follows automatically: one must verify separately that the intersection of 𝒱r−A\mathcal{V}_{r}-A with that sub-manifold is not the whole sub-manifold. This is precisely what is established for multi-head attention in Theorem 5.3 below.

5.2 Residual connections generically obstruct rank collapse

Theorem 5.3 (Generic residual obstruction of rank collapse).

Consider the map X(l+1)=X(l)+MHA⁡(X(l))X^{(l+1)}=X^{(l)}+\operatorname{MHA}(X^{(l)}) (attention with residual, no MLP). Fix weight matrices {WQ(h),WK(h),WV(h),WO(h)}\{W_{Q}^{(h)},W_{K}^{(h)},W_{V}^{(h)},W_{O}^{(h)}\}. Then for Lebesgue-almost-every input X(l)∈ℝn×dmodelX^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} with rank⁡(X(l))<min⁡(n,dmodel)\operatorname{rank}(X^{(l)})<\min(n,d_{\mathrm{model}}),

rank⁡(X(l)+MHA⁡(X(l)))>rank⁡(X(l)).\operatorname{rank}\bigl(X^{(l)}+\operatorname{MHA}(X^{(l)})\bigr)\;>\;\operatorname{rank}\bigl(X^{(l)}\bigr).

In particular, the doubly-exponential rank-collapse mechanism of residual-free attention [4] is generically obstructed by the residual connection. The result is generic, not deterministic: exact cancellation MHA⁡(X(l))=−X(l)\operatorname{MHA}(X^{(l)})=-X^{(l)} is possible in principle but constitutes a measure-zero event.

Proof.

The proof is in two steps: (a) characterise the bad set as an analytic subset of ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, and (b) exhibit one input outside it, so the bad set is proper and hence has Lebesgue measure zero.

Step (a): Algebraic characterisation of the bad set. Fix layer ll, fixed weights, and let X=X(l)X=X^{(l)}. Define the map

F⁡(X)=X+MHA⁡(X)=X+∑hA(h)​(X)​X​WV(h)​WO(h),F(X)\;=\;X+\operatorname{MHA}(X)\;=\;X+\sum_{h}A^{(h)}(X)\,XW_{V}^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)},

with A(h)​(X)=softmax⁡(S(h))A^{(h)}(X)=\operatorname{softmax}(S^{(h)}), Si​j(h)=xi​M(h)​xj⊤/dkS^{(h)}_{ij}=x_{i}M^{(h)}x_{j}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{k}}, and M(h)=WQ(h)​WK(h)⊤M^{(h)}=W_{Q}^{(h)}W_{K}^{(h)\top}. Both A(h)A^{(h)} and FF are real-analytic on the whole of ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} (the softmax is real-analytic, and analyticity is preserved under composition, sum, and product).

Define the bad set

ℬl={X∈ℝn×dmodel:rank⁡(F⁡(X))≤rank⁡(X)}.\mathcal{B}_{l}\;=\;\bigl\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}:\operatorname{rank}\bigl(F(X)\bigr)\leq\operatorname{rank}(X)\bigr\}.

This is precisely the locus on which the conclusion of the theorem fails. Stratifying by r=rank⁡(X)∈{0,1,…,min⁡(n,dmodel)−1}r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\in\{0,1,\dots,\min(n,d_{\mathrm{model}})-1\}, the bad set decomposes as the finite union ℬl=⋃rℬl(r)\mathcal{B}_{l}=\bigcup_{r}\mathcal{B}_{l}^{(r)} with

ℬl(r)={X:rank⁡(X)=r​ and ​rank⁡(F⁡(X))≤r}.\mathcal{B}_{l}^{(r)}\;=\;\bigl\{X:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\text{ and }\operatorname{rank}(F(X))\leq r\bigr\}.

The condition rank⁡(F⁡(X))≤r\operatorname{rank}(F(X))\leq r is the simultaneous vanishing of all (r+1)×(r+1)(r{+}1)\times(r{+}1) minors of F⁡(X)F(X), each of which is a real-analytic function of XX. Hence {X:rank⁡(F⁡(X))≤r}\{X:\operatorname{rank}(F(X))\leq r\} is a real-analytic subset of ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, and so is its intersection with {X:rank⁡(X)=r}\{X:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\}. Crucially, no use is made of the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, so analyticity is global and no stratum-by-stratum patching is required.

Step (b): The bad set is proper. A real-analytic subset of ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} either equals the entire space or has Lebesgue measure zero (Krantz and Parks [7], Chapter 1). It therefore suffices to exhibit a single X⋆∉ℬlX^{\star}\notin\mathcal{B}_{l}.

Explicit witness. Take X⋆=𝐞1​𝐟1⊤X^{\star}=\mathbf{e}_{1}\mathbf{f}_{1}^{\top}, which has rank 11. For generic weights, the output MHA⁡(X⋆)=∑hA(h)​(X⋆)​X⋆​WV(h)​WO(h)\operatorname{MHA}(X^{\star})=\sum_{h}A^{(h)}(X^{\star})\,X^{\star}W_{V}^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} has a non-zero component along directions outside span⁡(𝐟1)\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{f}_{1}): choosing WO(1)W_{O}^{(1)} whose first row has a non-zero entry in the second coordinate of ℝdmodel\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}} ensures that MHA⁡(X⋆)\operatorname{MHA}(X^{\star}) is not contained in span⁡(𝐟1)\mathrm{span}(\mathbf{f}_{1}) row-wise, and elementary computation shows rank⁡(X⋆+MHA⁡(X⋆))=2>1\operatorname{rank}(X^{\star}+\operatorname{MHA}(X^{\star}))=2>1 for almost every choice of WV(h),WO(h)W_{V}^{(h)},W_{O}^{(h)} (the configurations on which equality holds form a proper algebraic subset of weight space). This witness shows ℬl≠ℝn×dmodel\mathcal{B}_{l}\neq\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} in each stratum ℬl(r)\mathcal{B}_{l}^{(r)} with r<min⁡(n,dmodel)r<\min(n,d_{\mathrm{model}}) (the witness itself sits in ℬl(1)​c\mathcal{B}_{l}^{(1)\,c}, and an analogous rank-rr witness Xr⋆=∑i=1r𝐞i​𝐟i⊤X^{\star}_{r}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mathbf{e}_{i}\mathbf{f}_{i}^{\top} handles the other strata).

Therefore each ℬl(r)\mathcal{B}_{l}^{(r)} is a proper real-analytic subset of ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, hence of Lebesgue measure zero, and ℬl\mathcal{B}_{l} is the union of finitely many such sets. For Lebesgue-almost-every X(l)X^{(l)} with rank⁡(X(l))<min⁡(n,dmodel)\operatorname{rank}(X^{(l)})<\min(n,d_{\mathrm{model}}), we have X(l)∉ℬlX^{(l)}\notin\mathcal{B}_{l}, i.e. rank⁡(X(l+1))>rank⁡(X(l))\operatorname{rank}(X^{(l+1)})>\operatorname{rank}(X^{(l)}). The doubly-exponential collapse of Dong et al. [4] cannot occur. ∎

Remark 5.4.

The argument bypasses the Moore–Penrose projector and any constant-rank stratification: it works directly with the analyticity of F⁡(X)=X+MHA⁡(X)F(X)=X+\operatorname{MHA}(X) and the determinantal characterisation of rank⁡(F⁡(X))≤r\operatorname{rank}(F(X))\leq r via (r+1)×(r+1)(r{+}1)\times(r{+}1) minors. This both strengthens the statement (rank strictly increases, not merely “rowspace not contained in rowspace”) and simplifies the proof. The result is also quantitative: the bad set is nowhere dense, so a small absolutely continuous perturbation of any X∈ℬlX\in\mathcal{B}_{l} exits the bad set with probability one. This is the relevant sense of “generically obstructs rank collapse.”

5.3 What the MLP is necessary for

Proposition 5.5 (Local linearity of attention).

Fix an input X(0)∈ℝn×dmodelX^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} and let {A(l,h)​(X(0))}\{A^{(l,h)}(X^{(0)})\} denote the attention weight matrices evaluated at X(0)X^{(0)}. Then the map X(0)↦X(L)X^{(0)}\mapsto X^{(L)} is locally affine at X(0)X^{(0)}: its first-order (Jacobian) approximation around X(0)X^{(0)} is

X(L)≈X(0)​Φ​(X(0))+B⁡(X(0)),X^{(L)}\approx X^{(0)}\Phi(X^{(0)})+B(X^{(0)}), (4)

where Φ\Phi and BB depend on X(0)X^{(0)} through the frozen attention weights. In particular, the representation X(L)X^{(L)} cannot escape the affine hull of X(0)X^{(0)} to first order: non-linear excursions require higher-order terms, which attention alone — being a composition of softmax and linear maps — cannot generate as efficiently as an explicit non-linearity.

Proof.

For a single layer ll, the map fl:X↦X+MHA⁡(X)f_{l}:X\mapsto X+\operatorname{MHA}(X) is smooth. Its Jacobian at X0=X(l)​(X(0))X_{0}=X^{(l)}(X^{(0)}) is:

D​fl​(X0)=I+D⁡[MHA]​(X0),Df_{l}(X_{0})=I+D[\operatorname{MHA}](X_{0}), (5)

where D​[MHA]​(X0)D[\operatorname{MHA}](X_{0}) is the Jacobian of the multi-head attention map evaluated at X0X_{0}.

Jacobian of a single head. The output is Y(h)=A(h)​(X)⋅X​WV(h)Y^{(h)}=A^{(h)}(X)\cdot XW_{V}^{(h)}, where A(h)​(X)=softmax⁡(S(h)​(X))A^{(h)}(X)=\operatorname{softmax}(S^{(h)}(X)) and S(h)​(X)=X​WQ(h)​WK(h)​T​XT/dkS^{(h)}(X)=XW_{Q}^{(h)}W_{K}^{(h)T}X^{T}/\sqrt{d_{k}}. By the product rule:

D⁡[Y(h)​WO(h)]​(X0)​[δ​X]=(D⁡[A(h)]​(X0)​[δ​X])​X0​WV(h)​WO(h)+A0(h)​(δ​X)​WV(h)​WO(h),\begin{split}D[Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}](X_{0})[\delta X]&=\bigl(D[A^{(h)}](X_{0})[\delta X]\bigr)X_{0}W_{V}^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}\\ &\quad+A_{0}^{(h)}(\delta X)W_{V}^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)},\end{split}

where A0(h)=A(h)​(X0)A^{(h)}_{0}=A^{(h)}(X_{0}) is the attention weight matrix at X0X_{0}, and D⁡[A(h)]​(X0)​[δ​X]D[A^{(h)}](X_{0})[\delta X] is the Jacobian of the softmax-attention map. Both terms are linear in δ​X\delta X, confirming that the Jacobian exists and the local approximation is affine.

First-order expansion. Summing over heads and layers:

X(L)​(X(0)+δ​X)=X(L)​(X(0))+Φ⁡(X(0))​δ​X+O⁡(‖δ​X‖2),X^{(L)}(X^{(0)}+\delta X)=X^{(L)}(X^{(0)})+\Phi(X^{(0)})\,\delta X+O(\|\delta X\|^{2}),

where Φ(X(0))=DfL−1∘⋯∘Df0(X(0))\Phi(X^{(0)})=Df_{L-1}\circ\cdots\circ Df_{0}(X^{(0)}) is the product of per-layer Jacobians — a well-defined linear map. Writing B⁡(X(0))=X(L)​(X(0))B(X^{(0)})=X^{(L)}(X^{(0)}), the local affine approximation is X(L)≈X(0)​Φ+BX^{(L)}\approx X^{(0)}\Phi+B as stated. The explicit inductive derivation uses the chain rule applied layer by layer. ∎

Remark 5.6 (What local linearity implies).

The global map X(0)↦X(L)X^{(0)}\mapsto X^{(L)} is not globally affine: softmax attention is non-linear in X(0)X^{(0)}, and repeated layers compose these non-linearities. The proposition establishes that the first-order behaviour is affine, which means that infinitesimal perturbations to X(0)X^{(0)} propagate linearly. The MLP’s role is to provide a qualitatively different kind of non-linearity: the GeLU activation generates feature directions that lie outside the tangent space of the current representation, which attention layers alone cannot do efficiently.

Corollary 5.7 (MLP is necessary for non-linear generalisation).

In a neighbourhood of any fixed input X(0)X^{(0)}, the Jacobian of the map X(0)↦X(L)X^{(0)}\mapsto X^{(L)} produced by attention with residual (no MLP) is a linear map. The GeLU non-linearity of the MLP introduces curvature that is unavailable to any composition of attention and residual connections.

This gives a precise reformulation of the MLP’s role:

6 Head Specialisation and Rank Contraction

The results of §5 show that residual connections generically obstruct rank collapse and that the MLP’s necessary function is non-linear feature generation. This section identifies a third phenomenon that connects the two: rank contraction of the multi-head output, driven by head specialisation.

6.1 The rank of the multi-head output

The multi-head output is MHA⁡(X)=∑h=1HY(h)​WO(h)\operatorname{MHA}(X)=\sum_{h=1}^{H}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}, where Y(h)∈ℝn×dkY^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{k}} and WO(h)∈ℝdk×dmodelW_{O}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. Each summand Y(h)​WO(h)Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} has rank≤dk\operatorname{rank}\leq d_{k}. By subadditivity, rank⁡(MHA⁡(X))≤H​dk=dmodel\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X))\leq Hd_{k}=d_{\mathrm{model}}.

The question is when this bound is tight and when it is not.

Definition 6.1 (Subspace alignment).

The alignment of the multi-head output is:

αMHA=1−rank⁡(MHA⁡(X))H⋅maxh⁡rank⁡(Y(h)​WO(h)).\alpha_{\mathrm{MHA}}=1-\frac{\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X))}{H\cdot\max_{h}\operatorname{rank}(Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)})}. (6)

αMHA=0\alpha_{\mathrm{MHA}}=0 iff the head output subspaces are in general position (no alignment); αMHA=1−1/H\alpha_{\mathrm{MHA}}=1-1/H iff all heads write into the same one-dimensional subspace.

Proposition 6.2 (Rank of Multi-Head Output Subspace).

Let ℛh=rowspace⁡(Y(h)​WO(h))\mathcal{R}_{h}=\operatorname{rowspace}(Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}) be the output subspace of head hh. Then:

rank⁡(MHA⁡(X))=dim(∑h=1Hℛh)=dim(ℛ1+⋯+ℛH).\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X))=\dim\!\left(\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{R}_{h}\right)=\dim\!\left(\mathcal{R}_{1}+\cdots+\mathcal{R}_{H}\right). (7)

In particular:

  1. (i)

    Generic case: if {ℛh}\{\mathcal{R}_{h}\} are in general position, then rank⁡(MHA⁡(X))=min⁡(n,H​dk,dmodel)\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X))=\min(n,Hd_{k},d_{\mathrm{model}}).

  2. (ii)

    Specialised case: if heads specialise so that ℛh⊆𝒱\mathcal{R}_{h}\subseteq\mathcal{V} for a common subspace 𝒱⊊ℝdmodel\mathcal{V}\subsetneq\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}, then rank⁡(MHA⁡(X))≤dim𝒱≪dmodel\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X))\leq\dim\mathcal{V}\ll d_{\mathrm{model}}.

  3. (iii)

    Directional specialisation: if head hh is directional (large ‖Ma(h)‖F\|M_{a}^{(h)}\|_{F}), its output concentrates in the eigenplane of Ma(h)M_{a}^{(h)}, a two-dimensional subspace of ℝdk\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}. Under the output projection WO(h)W_{O}^{(h)}, this maps to a two-dimensional subspace of ℝdmodel\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}. HH directional heads contribute at most 2​H2H dimensions to rank⁡(MHA⁡(X))\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X)).

Proposition 6.3 (Architectural Bound on Head Output Rank).

Let WV(h)∈ℝdmodel×dkW_{V}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_{k}} and WO(h)∈ℝdk×dmodelW_{O}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} be generic weight matrices. For Lebesgue-almost-every input XX and attention matrix A(h)A^{(h)}:

dim(ℛh)=min⁡(rank⁡(X),dk).\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h})\;=\;\min\!\bigl(\operatorname{rank}(X),\;d_{k}\bigr).

In particular, dim(ℛh)\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h}) is independent of the directional asymmetry index αh(l)\alpha_{h}^{(l)}.

Proof.

The output subspace is determined by the chain X→WV(h)ℝn×dk→A(h)ℝn×dk→WO(h)ℝn×dmodelX\xrightarrow{W_{V}^{(h)}}\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{k}}\xrightarrow{A^{(h)}}\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{k}}\xrightarrow{W_{O}^{(h)}}\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}. For generic WV(h)W_{V}^{(h)}: rank⁡(X​WV(h))=min⁡(rank⁡(X),dk)\operatorname{rank}(XW_{V}^{(h)})=\min(\operatorname{rank}(X),d_{k}). The attention matrix A(h)A^{(h)} is a row-stochastic matrix of rank min⁡(n,dk)=dk\min(n,d_{k})=d_{k} generically (when n>dkn>d_{k}), so left-multiplication by A(h)A^{(h)} does not reduce rank. For generic WO(h)W_{O}^{(h)} of rank dkd_{k}, right-multiplication also preserves rank. Hence dim(ℛh)=min⁡(rank⁡(X),dk)\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h})=\min(\operatorname{rank}(X),d_{k}). Since αh\alpha_{h} affects only A(h)A^{(h)}, and A(h)A^{(h)} does not appear in the rank formula, the result is independent of αh\alpha_{h}. ∎

Remark 6.4 (Consequence for rank contraction).

Proposition 6.3 shows that head specialisation does not reduce the dimension of individual head output subspaces. What specialisation changes is the orientation of ℛh\mathcal{R}_{h}: directional and reciprocal heads write into equally-sized subspaces, but in different directions. Rank contraction of MHA⁡(X)=∑hY(h)​WO(h)\operatorname{MHA}(X)=\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} therefore arises from subspace alignment (the ℛh\mathcal{R}_{h} become parallel) rather than from dimensional reduction of individual subspaces. This is the corrected mechanistic picture.

Conjecture 6.5 (Directional Specialisation Induces Subspace Alignment).

When heads are directional (high αh(l)\alpha_{h}^{(l)}), their output subspaces ℛh\mathcal{R}_{h} tend to become aligned (pointing in similar directions in ℝdmodel\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}). Since dim(ℛh)=dk\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h})=d_{k} for each head individually (Proposition 6.3), the rank reduction of MHA⁡(X(l))=∑hY(h)​WO(h)\operatorname{MHA}(X^{(l)})=\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} occurs through dim(ℛ1+⋯+ℛH)<H​dk\dim(\mathcal{R}_{1}+\cdots+\mathcal{R}_{H})<Hd_{k}, i.e., through overlapping subspaces rather than shrinking ones. The correct experimental test correlates αh(l)\alpha_{h}^{(l)} with the principal angles between pairs (ℛh,ℛh′)(\mathcal{R}_{h},\mathcal{R}_{h^{\prime}}), not with dim(ℛh)\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h}) individually.

Proof.

Equation (7) is standard linear algebra: the row space of a sum equals the sum of the row spaces. Case (i): general position means ℛh∩∑k<hℛk={0}\mathcal{R}_{h}\cap\sum_{k<h}\mathcal{R}_{k}=\{0\} for each hh, so dimensions add. Case (ii): all ℛh⊆𝒱\mathcal{R}_{h}\subseteq\mathcal{V} implies ∑hℛh⊆𝒱\sum_{h}\mathcal{R}_{h}\subseteq\mathcal{V}. Case (iii): the canonical symplectic decomposition of Ma(h)M_{a}^{(h)} (see Cirrincione [1]) gives the active eigenplane structure; the output projection maps each eigenplane to a corresponding subspace of ℝdmodel\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}. ∎

6.2 The specialisation–contraction–expansion loop

The Rank Contraction Theorem reveals a per-layer loop (Figure 2):

Head specialisation ⇒\Rightarrow Subspace alignment
(large ‖Ma(h)‖F\|M_{a}^{(h)}\|_{F}, heads write (multiple heads write into
into eigenplane of Ma(h)M_{a}^{(h)}) overlapping subspaces)
⇑\Uparrow ⇓\Downarrow
MLP non-linear expansion ⇐\Leftarrow Rank contraction
(GeLU generates new feature (rank⁡(MHA⁡(X))≪dmodel\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X))\ll d_{\mathrm{model}};
directions outside current span) information is concentrated)

The loop has three corollaries:

Head specialisation
(large ‖Ma(h)‖F\|M_{a}^{(h)}\|_{F}) 		⇒\Rightarrow Subspace alignment

Specialised (directional) heads do not necessarily write into lower-dimensional subspaces: by Proposition 6.3, dim(ℛh)=min⁡(rank⁡(X),dk)\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h})=\min(\operatorname{rank}(X),d_{k}) regardless of the specialisation level αh\alpha_{h}. What specialisation does is orient the head output subspaces ℛh\mathcal{R}_{h} in increasingly aligned directions. Rank contraction in MHA⁡(X)=∑hY(h)​WO(h)\operatorname{MHA}(X)=\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} therefore arises only after summation, through overlap among the ℛh\mathcal{R}_{h}. The MLP then expands the representation back toward full rank via its non-linearity.

This loop has three corollaries:

Corollary 6.6 (Specialisation amplifies the need for MLP).

As head specialisation increases (measured by αh=‖Ma(h)‖F/‖M(h)‖F\alpha_{h}=\|M_{a}^{(h)}\|_{F}/\|M^{(h)}\|_{F}), the rank of MHA⁡(X)\operatorname{MHA}(X) decreases, and the MLP must generate more new directions to maintain full representational capacity. Architectures with more directional heads require larger dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} to compensate for the rank contraction they induce.

Corollary 6.7 (Optimal dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} depends on directional structure).

Let r=rank⁡(MHA⁡(X(l)))r=\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X^{(l)})) at a typical layer ll. To restore full-rank representations, the MLP must generate dmodel−rd_{\mathrm{model}}-r new independent directions via its non-linearity. The minimum dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} required satisfies:

dff⋆≥dmodel−r+dmodel= 2​dmodel−r.d_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\star}\;\geq\;d_{\mathrm{model}}-r+d_{\mathrm{model}}\;=\;2d_{\mathrm{model}}-r. (8)

For generic (unspecialised) heads: r≈dmodelr\approx d_{\mathrm{model}}, so dff⋆≈dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\star}\approx d_{\mathrm{model}} (i.e. ×1\times 1, not ×4\times 4). For fully directional heads: r≈2​H≪dmodelr\approx 2H\ll d_{\mathrm{model}}, so dff⋆≈2​dmodel−2​H≈2​dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\star}\approx 2d_{\mathrm{model}}-2H\approx 2d_{\mathrm{model}} (i.e. ×2\times 2).

Corollary 6.8 (Connection with the directional energy).

The residual directional energy Γres(l)=H−1​∑h‖Pa(l,h)‖F2\Gamma_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l)}=H^{-1}\sum_{h}\|P_{a}^{(l,h)}\|_{F}^{2} (introduced in Cirrincione [1] as the diagnostic for pre-training progress) is a proxy for dmodel−rank⁡(MHA⁡(X(l)))d_{\mathrm{model}}-\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{MHA}(X^{(l)})): high directional energy implies more subspace alignment, more rank contraction, and larger MLP expansion needed. This connects the pre-training analysis of Cirrincione [1] with the architectural analysis of the present paper.

Design implication for MLP width

The width bound (8) suggests that the canonical dff=4​dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}=4d_{\mathrm{model}} is not generally forced by rank considerations and may be larger than necessary in many regimes. For tasks with low non-linear complexity — such as classification from a pre-trained representation, where most of the work is already done by the encoder — a reduced width dff=2​dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}=2d_{\mathrm{model}} may suffice. A formal version of this argument, including a definition of non-linear complexity and the resulting optimal-dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} proposition, is given in A.

7 Head-Channel Non-Identifiability

7.1 The phenomenon

Rank collapse concerns the rank of the hidden-state matrix X(l)X^{(l)}. Head-channel non-identifiability concerns a different object: the identifiability of individual head contributions inside the multi-head sum.

Intuition

Given only the sum ∑hY(h)​WO(h)\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}, no subsequent layer can determine which head contributed which directions — infinitely many configurations produce the same sum. This is head-channel non-identifiability.

Definition 7.1 (Head-channel non-identifiability).

Recall MHA⁡(X)=∑hY(h)​WO(h)\operatorname{MHA}(X)=\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}, Y(h)=A(h)​X​WV(h)∈ℝn×dkY^{(h)}=A^{(h)}XW_{V}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{k}}. The output projection is said to induce head-channel non-identifiability when no downstream linear map Ψ\Psi can recover the contribution Y(h∗)​WO(h∗)Y^{(h^{*})}W_{O}^{(h^{*})} of a specific head h∗h^{*} from MHA⁡(X)\operatorname{MHA}(X) alone, without knowledge of the other head contributions.

Remark 7.2.

When H​dk=dmodelHd_{k}=d_{\mathrm{model}}, the joint map ϕ:(Y(h))h↦∑hY(h)​WO(h)\phi:(Y^{(h)})_{h}\mapsto\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} is generically bijective: no identification becomes ambiguous in the Shannon sense. What is lost is identifiability of the chosen decomposition: given only the mixture MHA⁡(X)\operatorname{MHA}(X), a downstream layer cannot determine which head produced which component. This is the precise sense in which head-channel non-identifiability operates. Thus, the non-identifiability considered here is not non-invertibility of the joint linear map, but the impossibility of canonically assigning a recovered component to a functional head without retaining the pre-summation head coordinates or fixing a gauge.

Theorem 7.3 (Head-Channel Non-Identifiability Theorem).

For any permutation π\pi of {1,…,H}\{1,\ldots,H\}, ∑hY(π⁡(h))​WO(π⁡(h))=∑hY(h)​WO(h)\sum_{h}Y^{(\pi(h))}W_{O}^{(\pi(h))}=\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} if and only if Y(h)​WO(h)=Y(π⁡(h))​WO(π⁡(h))Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}=Y^{(\pi(h))}W_{O}^{(\pi(h))} for all hh. Moreover, the map X↦MHA⁡(X)X\mapsto\operatorname{MHA}(X) has the same output for all assignments of head outputs to head indices that produce the same sum. The individual head contributions Y(h)​WO(h)Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} are not recoverable from MHA⁡(X)\operatorname{MHA}(X) by any downstream linear map.

Proof.

The sum ∑hY(h)​WO(h)\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} is invariant under rearrangement of the summands that preserves their values. For recovery: suppose Ψ⁡(∑hY(h)​WO(h))=Y(1)​WO(1)\Psi\bigl(\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}\bigr)=Y^{(1)}W_{O}^{(1)}. Then also Ψ⁡(∑hY(h)​WO(h)+Z)=Y(1)​WO(1)\Psi\bigl(\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}+Z\bigr)=Y^{(1)}W_{O}^{(1)} for any ZZ in the null space of Ψ\Psi. Take Z=−Y(1)​WO(1)+Y′(1)​WO(1)Z=-Y^{(1)}W_{O}^{(1)}+Y^{\prime(1)}W_{O}^{(1)} with Y′(1)≠Y(1)Y^{\prime(1)}\neq Y^{(1)} but Y′(1)​WO(1)=Y(1)​WO(1)Y^{\prime(1)}W_{O}^{(1)}=Y^{(1)}W_{O}^{(1)} (possible since WO(1)W_{O}^{(1)} has rank dk<dmodeld_{k}<d_{\mathrm{model}}): contradiction. See the proof of Theorem 7.6 below. ∎

7.2 Why the MLP cannot help

Proposition 7.4 (MLP acts post-destruction).

The MLP in a standard Transformer block receives as input X(l)+MHA⁡(X(l))X^{(l)}+\operatorname{MHA}(X^{(l)}): the hidden state after the multi-head sum has been formed. Any features the MLP generates are functions of this mixture. It has no access to the individual head outputs Y(h)Y^{(h)}.

This is not a criticism of the MLP — it is an architectural observation. The MLP does its job (non-linear feature generation) on the post-destruction mixture. Addressing head-channel non-identifiability requires an intervention before the sum, not after.

7.3 The recovery ambiguity dimension of head-channel non-identifiability

The Head-Channel Non-Identifiability Theorem establishes that individual head contributions are irrecoverable. We now quantify how much identification becomes ambiguous.

Definition 7.5 (Recovery subspace).

Fix head h∗∈{1,…,H}h^{*}\in\{1,\ldots,H\}. The recovery subspace for h∗h^{*} is:

𝒦h∗=ker⁡((Y(1),…,Y(H))↦Y(h∗)​WO(h∗)|∑hY(h)​WO(h)=𝟎),\mathcal{K}_{h^{*}}=\ker\!\left((Y^{(1)},\ldots,Y^{(H)})\mapsto Y^{(h^{*})}W_{O}^{(h^{*})}\;\Big|\;\textstyle\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}=\mathbf{0}\right), (9)

the set of head-output configurations that are invisible in the multi-head sum and that contaminate the recovery of head h∗h^{*}.

Theorem 7.6 (Recovery Ambiguity Theorem).

For generic {WO(h)}h≠h∗\{W_{O}^{(h)}\}_{h\neq h^{*}} with rank⁡(WO(h))=dk\operatorname{rank}(W_{O}^{(h)})=d_{k} for all hh:

dim𝒦h∗=n⁡(H−1)​dk.\dim\,\mathcal{K}_{h^{*}}=n(H-1)d_{k}. (10)

Recovering the contribution of any single head from the multi-head output requires knowledge of n⁡(H−1)​dkn(H-1)d_{k} additional degrees of freedom — the contributions of all other heads.

For BertBase (n=512n=512, H=12H=12, dk=64d_{k}=64):

dim𝒦h∗=512×11×64=360,448.\dim\,\mathcal{K}_{h^{*}}=512\times 11\times 64=360{,}448. (11)

This is the dimension of the non-identifiability subspace for the full sequence at one layer. Per token, the corresponding quantity is (H−1)​dk=11×64=704(H-1)d_{k}=11\times 64=704.

Proof.

The joint map ϕ:(Y(1),…,Y(H))↦∑hY(h)​WO(h)\phi:(Y^{(1)},\ldots,Y^{(H)})\mapsto\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} operates on a space of dimension n​H​dknHd_{k} and maps to n​dmodelnd_{\mathrm{model}}. For BertBase, H​dk=dmodelHd_{k}=d_{\mathrm{model}}, so ϕ\phi is generically bijective (kernel dimension 00) as a joint map.

Now fix ∑hY(h)​WO(h)=S\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}=S (the observed output) and ask: what is the space of (Y(1),…,Y(H))(Y^{(1)},\ldots,Y^{(H)}) consistent with SS? This is the affine preimage ϕ−1​(S)\phi^{-1}(S), which (since ϕ\phi is bijective) contains exactly one point. But the question of recovering Y(h∗)​WO(h∗)Y^{(h^{*})}W_{O}^{(h^{*})} from SS alone is different: it requires inverting the marginal map ψh∗:Y(h∗)↦S−∑h≠h∗Y(h)​WO(h)\psi_{h^{*}}:Y^{(h^{*})}\mapsto S-\sum_{h\neq h^{*}}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}, where the second term is unknown.

The uncertainty set for ∑h≠h∗Y(h)​WO(h)\sum_{h\neq h^{*}}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} lives in ℝn×dmodel\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}, parametrised by (H−1)(H-1) independent blocks each of dimension n​dknd_{k}. For generic {WO(h)}h≠h∗\{W_{O}^{(h)}\}_{h\neq h^{*}}, these blocks span a subspace of dimension n⁡(H−1)​dkn(H-1)d_{k} in the space of n×dmodeln\times d_{\mathrm{model}} matrices. This is 𝒦h∗\mathcal{K}_{h^{*}}, and its dimension is (10). ∎

Remark 7.7 (Design implication).

Equation (10) shows that the recovery ambiguity dimension of head-channel non-identifiability scales as n⁡(H−1)​dk=n⁡(dmodel−dk)n(H-1)d_{k}=n(d_{\mathrm{model}}-d_{k}). It grows linearly with sequence length nn and is minimised when H=1H=1 (a single head, zero cost) or when dk=dmodeld_{k}=d_{\mathrm{model}} (full dimension per head, zero compression). The standard BERT choice H=dmodel/dk=12H=d_{\mathrm{model}}/d_{k}=12 maximises both the number of specialised heads and the recovery ambiguity dimension of their mixing. PG-OP partially addresses this by making the gate gh​(xi,i)g_{h}(x_{i},i) position-dependent, so that the effective mixing coefficients vary with ii — reducing the effective dimension of the uncertainty set at each position.

7.4 Table: what each component does

8 Design Implication: Position-Gated Output Projection

8.1 Motivation

Head-channel non-identifiability arises because WO(h)W_{O}^{(h)} applies the same linear map to every token position ii: the contribution of head hh at position ii is Yi(h)​WO(h)Y_{i}^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}, independent of ii. This position-invariance is exactly the mechanism that makes the contributions unidentifiable.

A natural remedy is to modulate the output projection by position.

8.2 Definition

Definition 8.1 (Position-Gated Output Projection, PG-OP).

Replace the standard output projection MHA⁡(X)i=∑hYi(h)​WO(h)\operatorname{MHA}(X)_{i}=\sum_{h}Y_{i}^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} with:

MHAPG⁡(X)i=∑h=1Hgh​(xi,i)⋅Yi(h)​WO(h),\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{PG}}(X)_{i}=\sum_{h=1}^{H}g_{h}(x_{i},i)\cdot Y_{i}^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}, (12)

where gh:ℝdmodel×{1,…,n}→(0,1)g_{h}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\times\{1,\ldots,n\}\to(0,1) is a position-gating function:

gh​(xi,i)=σ⁡(xi​Wg(h)+pi​wp(h)+bg(h)),g_{h}(x_{i},i)=\sigma\!\left(x_{i}W_{g}^{(h)}+p_{i}w_{p}^{(h)}+b_{g}^{(h)}\right), (13)

with Wg(h)∈ℝdmodel×1W_{g}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times 1}, pi∈ℝdpep_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{pe}}} the positional encoding of position ii, wp(h)∈ℝdpew_{p}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{pe}}}, and σ=sigmoid\sigma=\mathrm{sigmoid}.

Parameter overhead for BertBase: H⁡(dmodel+dpe+1)=12×(768+768+1)≈18,408H(d_{\mathrm{model}}+d_{\mathrm{pe}}+1)=12\times(768+768+1)\approx 18{,}408 parameters, less than 1.6% of WOW_{O}’s dmodel2=589,824d_{\mathrm{model}}^{2}=589{,}824 parameters.

Empirical prediction

PG-OP strictly contains standard MHA\operatorname{MHA} as a parameter subfamily (constant gate gh≡1g_{h}\equiv 1 recovers MHA\operatorname{MHA}); the larger family suggests — but does not prove — that there exist tasks on which MHAPG\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{PG}} attains lower loss than the best achievable by standard MHA\operatorname{MHA}. An expressiveness analysis is given in B. A more specific empirical prediction relates the gate to the directional asymmetry of each head:

Proposition 8.2 (Gate correlates with directional asymmetry).

Let αh(l)=‖Ma(l,h)‖F/‖M(l,h)‖F\alpha_{h}^{(l)}=\|M_{a}^{(l,h)}\|_{F}/\|M^{(l,h)}\|_{F} be the directional asymmetry index of head hh at layer ll. Under the hypothesis that directional heads (high αh\alpha_{h}) benefit more from position-dependent gating:

Pearson⁡(αh(l),𝔼i​[|∂gh​(xi,i)∂i|])>0.6\mathrm{Pearson}\!\left(\alpha_{h}^{(l)},\;\mathbb{E}_{i}\!\left[\left|\tfrac{\partial g_{h}(x_{i},i)}{\partial i}\right|\right]\right)>0.6 (14)

at each layer ll of a fine-tuned BertBase+PG-OP model on GLUE.

This prediction distinguishes PG-OP from random gating and provides a concrete experimental test for the head-channel non-identifiability hypothesis.

9 A Unified Framework: Symmetry-Breaking and Representational Collapse

The results of §§4–6 can be unified under a single principle: every collapse phenomenon in the Transformer corresponds to a symmetry that the architecture fails to break.

9.1 Symmetries of the forward pass

A map gg is a forward-pass symmetry if f⁡(g⁡(X))=f⁡(X)f(g(X))=f(X) for all XX, where ff is the Transformer’s forward pass. A collapse phenomenon arises when the architecture fails to break a symmetry that the task requires to be broken. The four collapse phenomena correspond to four distinct symmetries:

9.2 The Symmetry-Breaking Framework

The four collapse phenomena above are not independent observations but instances of a single principle: each is the unbroken (or partially broken) action of a symmetry group on the forward pass. A formal definition of the invariance group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, its three relevant subgroups 𝒢depth\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{depth}}, 𝒢channel\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{channel}}, 𝒢LN\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{LN}}, and a proof sketch that they commute (act on orthogonal degrees of freedom) is given in C. The architectural implications of the framework, however, can be stated immediately and are the most useful consequence for designers.

Remark 9.1 (Architectural implications).

If the Symmetry-Breaking Decomposition framework is accepted as a working hypothesis, the design question “what components does a Transformer need?” becomes an algebraic question: “what symmetries does the target task require to be broken?”

A task that requires distinguishing token identity from token position needs to break 𝒢depth\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{depth}}: residual connections are necessary.

A task requiring head-specialised output routing needs to break 𝒢channel\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{channel}}: PG-OP or an equivalent mechanism is necessary.

A task whose target function is scale-invariant can tolerate 𝒢LN\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{LN}}: LN does not need to be removed.

The canonical Transformer breaks 𝒢depth\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{depth}} (via residual) but not 𝒢channel\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{channel}} (standard WOW_{O} is gauge-invariant and permutation-invariant). This is the precise algebraic reason why head-channel non-identifiability is structural and not accidental.

10 Empirical Validation

Four experiments validate the main theoretical results. The two experiments most directly tied to the central thesis are reported in full here: residual stability (Theorem 5.3) and the 𝒢channel\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{channel}} gauge symmetry (Theorem 7.3). The two remaining experiments — numerical rank-neutrality (Theorem 4.2) and the null result on αh\alpha_{h} vs. MHA rank (Proposition 6.3) — are reported in D together with the parametric simulation of Figure 8. Experiments 1 and 2 use BertBase on the WikiText-2 validation corpus [14] (Kaggle P100 GPU); Experiment 3 is an algebraic-numerical verification requiring no GPU; Experiment 4 uses BertBase weight matrices on a Colab A100 GPU.

Experiment 2: Residual stability

Two BertBase variants are compared layer by layer: standard (with residual connections) and a patched version where the residual is zeroed via forward pre-hooks on BertSelfOutput and BertOutput.

Figure 4 confirms Theorem 5.3. With residual connections, rank remains 63.7±0.4563.7\pm 0.45 through layer 12. Without residual connections, rank collapses from 64 to 1 by layer 6 and remains at 1 thereafter (std = 0 from layer 6: the collapse is deterministic across all sentences).

Experiment 3: 𝒢channel\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{channel}} gauge symmetry

The Head-Channel Non-Identifiability Theorem asserts that for any Ah∈G​L​(dk)A_{h}\in GL(d_{k}), the substitution WV(h)→WV(h)​AhW_{V}^{(h)}\to W_{V}^{(h)}A_{h}, WO(h)→Ah−1​WO(h)W_{O}^{(h)}\to A_{h}^{-1}W_{O}^{(h)} leaves MHA⁡(X)\operatorname{MHA}(X) unchanged. This identity is verified numerically using BertBase-scale random weight matrices (d=768d=768, H=12H=12, dk=64d_{k}=64): 50 independent random Ah∈G​L​(dk)A_{h}\in GL(d_{k}) are drawn at each of 7 scales (condition numbers from e0.2e^{0.2} to e20e^{20}) and applied simultaneously to all 12 heads.

Figure 5 shows that the relative error

‖MHAgauged−MHAorig‖F/‖MHAorig‖F=1.84×10−15\|\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{gauged}}-\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{orig}}\|_{F}\,/\,\|\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{orig}}\|_{F}=1.84\times 10^{-15}

(mean, across all scales and all head counts). The invariance is exact: the sole source of error is floating-point rounding, confirming that 𝒢channel\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{channel}} is an exact symmetry of the MHA forward pass.

11 Discussion

Relationship with Dong et al

Dong’s result is tight in its regime: pure attention, no residual, no MLP. The study concerns the regime of deployed Transformers: with residual connections, with MLP, with layer normalisation. The results are complementary: Dong characterises the degenerate regime; a characterisation is given the mechanisms that prevent degeneracy and identify which of them is actually necessary.

Relationship with the MLP-as-key-value memory line

Geva et al. [6] interpret MLP layers as key-value memories storing factual knowledge. The analysis is orthogonal: we ask about the MLP’s structural role in rank maintenance, not its functional role in knowledge storage. Both views can be simultaneously correct.

Sparse and structured MLP variants

Mixture-of-experts [11] and sparse MLP [5] reduce dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} selectively. The design corollary of §6 (formal version in A) provides a theoretical motivation for this direction: dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} should match task non-linear complexity, and sparse activation is one mechanism for achieving this.

Head-channel non-identifiability and pre-mixing intervention

A complete remedy for head-channel non-identifiability requires intervening before the summation. The PG-OP of §8 is a lightweight, drop-in partial remedy within the existing architecture.

A taxonomy of four collapse phenomena

Figure 1 summarises the four distinct phenomena and their relationships; §9 shows they arise as orbits of distinct unbroken symmetries of the forward pass. The “tug of war” framing of Dong captures only phenomenon (i); a complete theory must address all four.

12 Directions for further work

Several questions raised by the analysis above remain open and define natural directions for further work.

Affine rank under row-wise rescaling

Step 2 of the Rank-Neutrality Theorem proof rescales each row by 1/σi>01/\sigma_{i}>0 and claims arank⁡(D​X~)=arank⁡(X~)\operatorname{arank}(D\tilde{X})=\operatorname{arank}(\tilde{X}). A complete analysis shows that this fails if and only if σ=(σ1,…,σn)⊤∈colspace​(X~)\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{n})^{\top}\in\text{colspace}(\tilde{X}): in that case there exists v≠0v\neq 0 such that X~​v=c​σ\tilde{X}v=c\,\sigma, making the rescaled rows affinely dependent in a direction they were not before. The condition σ∉colspace​(X~)\sigma\notin\text{colspace}(\tilde{X}) can be added as hypothesis H4; it holds generically when n>dn>d (the typical case, since colspace​(X~)⊆ℝn\text{colspace}(\tilde{X})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} has dimension at most d≪nd\ll n). The theorem is unconditional under H1–H4.

A unifying symmetry groupoid

The framework of C identifies three symmetries, but 𝒢channel\mathcal{G}_{\rm channel} and 𝒢depth\mathcal{G}_{\rm depth} act on parameters and limit dynamics respectively, while 𝒢LN\mathcal{G}_{\rm LN} acts on inputs. These are symmetries of different objects. For the forward-pass invariance group acting on inputs, one can show that with generic weights and a softmax non-linearity, the group is generically trivial (only the identity), because the map X↦A(h)​(X)​X​WV(h)​WO(h)X\mapsto A^{(h)}(X)XW_{V}^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} is generically injective. A unifying framework would be a parametrised symmetry groupoid that acts jointly on inputs and parameters, capturing all three types. Constructing this groupoid precisely is left to future work.

Principal angles between head subspaces

Proposition 6.3 resolves the strong form of Conjecture 6.5: dim(ℛh)=min⁡(rank⁡(X),dk)\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h})=\min(\operatorname{rank}(X),d_{k}) is independent of αh\alpha_{h}. Head specialisation does not shrink individual output subspaces; it aligns them. A natural next question is whether directional heads (αh\alpha_{h} high) produce more aligned pairs (ℛh,ℛh′)(\mathcal{R}_{h},\mathcal{R}_{h^{\prime}}) than reciprocal heads. The correct test measures the principal angles θ1≤⋯≤θdk\theta_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\theta_{d_{k}} between pairs of output subspaces, and correlates αh\alpha_{h} with cos2⁡θ1\cos^{2}\theta_{1} (the maximal alignment). This experiment requires per-head output extraction and subspace angle computation, feasible without additional GPU time on the existing BERT-base setup.

Empirical validation of PG-OP

The expressiveness analysis of B shows that PG-OP contains standard MHA as a parameter subfamily. Whether the larger parameter space reduces task loss on GLUE or WikiText-2 is an empirical question to be settled in companion work.

Rank dynamics during training

Theorem 5.3 is a static result on a single forward pass. Whether the effective rank of X(l)X^{(l)} increases, decreases, or oscillates during training, and whether head specialisation drives rank contraction in the trained model relative to random initialisation, remains to be determined.

Non-linear recovery of head contributions

The Recovery Ambiguity Theorem concerns linear reconstruction. Whether non-linear decoders reduce the ambiguity dimension, and at what representational cost, is an open question. A precise quantitative relationship between the degree of symmetry breaking (e.g., via PG-OP) and the reduction in ambiguity dimension would make the framework constructive.

13 Conclusion

Dong et al. (2021) identified a real phenomenon and proposed a real remedy, but the analysis was conducted in a regime that does not describe any deployed architecture. In real Transformers with residual connections, the three components implicated in rank collapse play different roles. Layer normalisation is rank-neutral under H1–H4: it preserves rank exactly. Residual connections generically obstruct rank collapse for almost every input. The MLP’s contribution is not anti-collapse but anti-confinement: without it, representations remain locally affine, unable to exploit the non-linear capacity that attention cannot provide.

The identification of head-channel non-identifiability as a phenomenon distinct from rank collapse is the most practically consequential result. After MHA⁡(X)=∑hY(h)​WO(h)\operatorname{MHA}(X)=\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)}, the per-head contributions cannot be canonically recovered from the mixture alone: n⁡(H−1)​dkn(H-1)d_{k} degrees of freedom remain ambiguous when recovering a single head contribution from the mixed output. The MLP cannot remedy this because it arrives too late.

The Symmetry-Breaking Decomposition Theorem provides a framework in which all four collapse phenomena in the literature correspond to distinct unbroken symmetries of the forward pass. This algebraic perspective converts architectural design questions into precise mathematical questions about which symmetries a given task requires to be broken. The Position-Gated Output Projection is a minimal, drop-in intervention that partially breaks the head-permutation symmetry responsible for head-channel non-identifiability, at a parameter cost below 1.6% of WOW_{O}.

Appendix A Width bounds from rank contraction

This appendix expands the design implication for MLP width sketched at the end of §6. The argument is a direct corollary of Corollary 5.7 (the MLP’s role is non-linear feature generation, not anti-collapse): if non-linearity is the MLP’s purpose, then dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} should be determined by the non-linear complexity of the task, not by the heuristic dff=4​dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}=4d_{\mathrm{model}}.

Definition A.1 (Non-linear complexity).

The non-linear complexity ν⁡(𝒯)\nu(\mathcal{T}) of a task 𝒯\mathcal{T} is the minimum dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} such that a single-hidden-layer network with dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} units achieves within ϵ\epsilon of the best achievable performance with any dff′>dffd_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\prime}>d_{\mathrm{ff}}.

Proposition A.2 (Optimal dffd_{\mathrm{ff}}).

Under the non-linear complexity hypothesis, the optimal dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} satisfies

dff⋆=min⁡{dff≥dmodel:ℒ⁡(dff)≤ℒ⁡(dff⋆)+ϵ},d_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\star}\;=\;\min\!\left\{d_{\mathrm{ff}}\geq d_{\mathrm{model}}:\mathcal{L}(d_{\mathrm{ff}})\leq\mathcal{L}(d_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\star})+\epsilon\right\}, (15)

which is task-dependent and in general ≠4​dmodel\neq 4d_{\mathrm{model}}. For tasks with low non-linear complexity (e.g. classification from pre-trained representations), dff⋆≪4​dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\star}\ll 4d_{\mathrm{model}}.

Empirical prediction

A reduced-MLP architecture with dff=2​dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}=2d_{\mathrm{model}} plus PG-OP (§8) achieves the same accuracy as standard dff=4​dmodeld_{\mathrm{ff}}=4d_{\mathrm{model}} on GLUE benchmarks, at 57%57\% of the FLOPs. This prediction is empirically testable and is the subject of companion experiments.

Appendix B PG-OP: expressiveness analysis

This appendix gives the formal expressiveness statement for PG-OP (§8) and the discussion of the empirical-prediction motivation, which were summarised inline in the main text.

Proposition B.1 (PG-OP contains standard MHA as a parameter subfamily).

Standard multi-head attention MHA\operatorname{MHA} is recovered from MHAPG\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{PG}} by setting gh≡1g_{h}\equiv 1 for all hh. Hence the parameter family of MHAPG\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{PG}} strictly contains that of MHA\operatorname{MHA}.

Proof.

The inclusion is immediate from Definition 8.1: the constant gate gh≡1g_{h}\equiv 1 reduces MHAPG\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{PG}} to standard MHA\operatorname{MHA}. Strictness follows from the fact that any non-constant position-dependent gate produces an output not realisable by any choice of MHA\operatorname{MHA} weights, since standard MHA\operatorname{MHA} has no position-dependence in the per-head output projection. ∎

Empirical-prediction motivation

The strictly larger parameter family suggests, but does not prove, that there exist tasks on which MHAPG\operatorname{MHA}_{\mathrm{PG}} attains lower loss than the best achievable by standard MHA\operatorname{MHA}. A natural candidate is any task whose optimal strategy weights head hh at position ii in proportion to that head’s directional energy Γ(h,i)\Gamma^{(h,i)} at position ii — a position-dependent quantity that constant gates cannot track. Whether this gain materialises in practice on standard benchmarks is an empirical question, addressed in Section 10 and stated more precisely in Proposition 8.2.

Appendix C Symmetry-breaking framework: formal definitions

This appendix gives the formal definitions and proof sketch for the symmetry-breaking framework introduced informally in §9.

Definition C.1 (Symmetry group of the forward pass).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be the group of all invertible maps g:ℝn×dmodel→ℝn×dmodelg:\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\mathrm{model}}} such that f⁡(g⁡(X))=f⁡(X)f(g(X))=f(X) for all XX and all weight configurations. 𝒢\mathcal{G} is called the invariance group of the Transformer.

Proposition C.2 (Symmetry-Breaking Framework).

The following is a structural framework, not a fully proved theorem: certain parts are established rigorously (see proof sketch below), while the full group-theoretic characterisation remains conjectural.

The invariance group 𝒢\mathcal{G} of the standard Transformer (attention + residual + LN, without MLP) contains at minimum the following subgroups:

  1. (i)

    𝒢depth≅𝒮dmodel⊗L\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{depth}}\cong\mathcal{S}_{d_{\mathrm{model}}}^{\otimes L}: the group generated by row-averaging maps in each layer (responsible for rank collapse in depth).

  2. (ii)

    𝒢channel≅𝔖H⋉(GL⁡(dk))H\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{channel}}\cong\mathfrak{S}_{H}\ltimes(\mathrm{GL}(d_{k}))^{H}: the group of head permutations composed with gauge transformations (responsible for head-channel non-identifiability).

  3. (iii)

    𝒢LN≅(ℝ>0)n×ℝn\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{LN}}\cong(\mathbb{R}_{>0})^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}: the group of row-wise rescalings and shifts (the exact symmetry that the Rank-Neutrality Theorem characterises).

These subgroups are mutually commuting (act on orthogonal degrees of freedom). Their joint action partitions the space of inputs into orbits that constitute the distinct collapse types. An architectural component breaks symmetry gg if and only if it renders the output dependent on the orbit representative, not just the orbit.

Proof sketch.

(i) Without residual or MLP, the attention map sends each row xi(l+1)=∑jAi​j(l)​xj(l)​WV(l)​WO(l)x_{i}^{(l+1)}=\sum_{j}A_{ij}^{(l)}x_{j}^{(l)}W_{V}^{(l)}W_{O}^{(l)}, which is a row-averaging operation. The group generated by such maps contains the uniform-average map (the fixed point of rank collapse) and hence the symmetry claimed. The residual connection breaks this symmetry by adding xi(l)x_{i}^{(l)} back.

(ii) The map ϕ:(Y(h))↦∑hY(h)​WO(h)\phi:(Y^{(h)})\mapsto\sum_{h}Y^{(h)}W_{O}^{(h)} is invariant under simultaneous transformation Y(h)→Y(h)​AhY^{(h)}\to Y^{(h)}A_{h}, WO(h)→Ah−1​WO(h)W_{O}^{(h)}\to A_{h}^{-1}W_{O}^{(h)} for any Ah∈GL⁡(dk)A_{h}\in\mathrm{GL}(d_{k}) — the gauge freedom identified in Cirrincione [1]. It is also invariant under head permutation composed with the corresponding weight permutation. The joint group is 𝔖H⋉(GL⁡(dk))H\mathfrak{S}_{H}\ltimes(\mathrm{GL}(d_{k}))^{H}. PG-OP breaks this symmetry partially by making the gate gh​(xi,i)g_{h}(x_{i},i) dependent on the head index hh in a position-specific way.

(iii) LN applies xi↦(xi−μi)/σix_{i}\mapsto(x_{i}-\mu_{i})/\sigma_{i}: row-wise rescaling and shifting. The Rank-Neutrality Theorem shows this map is rank-preserving, which means it is in 𝒢LN\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{LN}} from the perspective of rank. Residual connections break 𝒢LN\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{LN}} by anchoring the representation to the original scale via the skip path.

Commutativity: (i) acts on the row-averaging structure of A(l)A^{(l)}; (ii) acts on the head-decomposition of WOW_{O}; (iii) acts on the row-normalisation of XX. These are orthogonal degrees of freedom and their actions commute. □\square ∎

Appendix D Additional experimental details

This appendix gives the two experiments not reported in the main text: the numerical Rank-Neutrality validation (Experiment 1, Theorem 4.2) and the specialisation-index vs. MHA-rank null result (Experiment 4, Proposition 6.3). A parametric simulation that complements Experiment 4 is also included.

Experiment 1: Rank-Neutrality Theorem

For each layer l=0,…,12l=0,\ldots,12, the numerical rank of X(l)X^{(l)} and LN⁡(X(l))\operatorname{LN}(X^{(l)}) is measured (threshold ε=10−3​σ1\varepsilon=10^{-3}\sigma_{1}) under two conditions: standard scale parameters γ=𝟏\gamma=\mathbf{1} (H1–H3 satisfied) and γj=0\gamma_{j}=0 for a random 50% of dimensions (H3 violated).

Figure 6 confirms Theorem 4.2. The mean absolute difference |rank⁡(X(l))−rank⁡(LN⁡(X(l)))||\operatorname{rank}(X^{(l)})-\operatorname{rank}(\operatorname{LN}(X^{(l)}))| is 0.0410.041 under H1–H4 and 0.0360.036 with H3 violated, both consistent with numerical thresholding at full rank (dk=64d_{k}=64). No systematic rank reduction is observed in either condition.

Experiment 4: Specialisation index vs. MHA rank (null result, by design)

The directional asymmetry index αh(l)=‖Ma(l,h)‖F/‖M(l,h)‖F\alpha_{h}^{(l)}=\|M_{a}^{(l,h)}\|_{F}/\|M^{(l,h)}\|_{F} is computed from BertBase weight matrices. The effective rank of MHA⁡(X(l))\operatorname{MHA}(X^{(l)}) is measured per layer on WikiText-2 (128 sentences, sequence length 48).

Figure 7 shows a weak positive correlation (r=+0.152r=+0.152, p=0.068p=0.068). Under the original “rank contraction via dimension shrinkage” reading, a negative correlation r<−0.3r<-0.3 would have been expected. Proposition 6.3 now explains the null result: dim(ℛh)\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h}) is determined architecturally (min⁡(rank⁡(X),dk)\min(\operatorname{rank}(X),d_{k})) and does not depend on αh\alpha_{h}, so no correlation with the full MHA rank should be expected from this mechanism. The correct experimental probe is to measure principal angles between the head subspaces ℛh\mathcal{R}_{h}, which test the subspace alignment mechanism formalised in Conjecture 6.5. We leave this measurement to future work; it requires per-layer SVD of each WO(h)W_{O}^{(h)}-image and pairwise principal-angle computation, which goes beyond the scope of the present scalar-correlation analysis.

Parametric simulation

A controlled parametric simulation confirms the theory (Figure 8). Sweeping αh\alpha_{h} from 0 (reciprocal) to 1 (directional) while holding all other weights fixed shows: (a) rank of X(l)X^{(l)} is stable at n=32n=32 for all αh\alpha_{h} with residual connections; (b) without residual connections, rank collapses to 1 regardless of αh\alpha_{h}; (c) dim(ℛh)=dk=16\dim(\mathcal{R}_{h})=d_{k}=16 for all αh\alpha_{h}, confirming Proposition 6.3 numerically.
